Wednesday, 6 July 2016
Religion and Science
Religion and Science are diametrically opposed to each other. They are poles apart, and it is nonsense to say that they compliment each other.

1. Religion says that there is a supernatural entity called God, which is immortal, permanent, all powerful, merciful, all good, etc

Science does not believe in supernatural entities. It does not believe anything in the Universe is permanent. Everything is changing and in flux, in accordance with some laws, which can be discovered by scientific research.

Science holds that there are no supernatural entities like God, angels, fairies, demons,witches or soul ( and therefore there is no such thing as transmigration of the soul, or resurrection on Judgment Day ), and that nothing is permanent, everything is changing, and in a state of flux, in accordance with certain laws which can be discovered by scientific research.

Science holds that the only reality is matter, which is in motion according to certain laws.
Some people ask : who created matter ? The answer is : there is no creator of matter. Matter came from matter, though the form keeps changing.

2. With every step science advances, religion recedes. Thus, people at one time thought that small pox is due to the anger of a goddess ( mata ), but now we know it is because of a virus, and can be prevented by innoculation. People at one time thought that rains are caused by a rain god, Indra, and so if there is drought we have to propitiate that god in some way ( many people in India still believe that ). Today we know that rains are caused by the build up of low pressure areas over a heated land. People at one time believed that Adam and Eve were created by God. Later Darwin proved that men evolved from the apes.

3. Religion relies on faith and divine revelation.
Science relies on observation, experiment and reason.

4. Religion claims to say the final word, and cannot be changed. Thus, the Vedas, the Quran, the Bible, etc cannot be changed.
In science there is no final word, and scientific theories can, and have been, regularly tested and changed.

For example, Newton said in 1666 that light travelled as particles ( the corpuscular theory ). But in
1678 the Dutch scientist Huygens' propunded his Fresnel principle that light travelled as waves. Much later Max Planck propounded his Quantum theory which said that light travelled as discrete particles. Still later, Quantum mechanics, as propounded by De Broglie, and as developed by Heisenberg, Schrodinger, etc, said that particles can be conceived of as waves ( and vice versa )

5. Religion says that the Universe was created at a particular time by God, with all living beings. But Darwin proved by his theory of evolution, that creatures have evolved.

6. Religion says that there has to be a Creator of the Universe, which is God.

Science says that there is no such Creator. The only reality in the Universe is matter ( or rather matter-energy, since matter and energy are two forms of the same substance, as Einstein proved ), and matter is in motion, in accordance with certain laws, which can be discovered by scientific research. If it is asked where did matter come from, the answer is matter came from matter.

If it is said that every thing must have a creator, then that creator too must have a creator. i.e. a super creator, and that super creator too must have a creator, i.e. a super super creator, and so on. This is known as the fallacy of the infinite regress.

7. Religion says that God is all powerful, merciful and all good. If that is so, then why do millions of children in the world suffer from hunger, cold, etc ? Why does God, who is said to be merciful, not have mercy on them and give them food, clothes, shelter, etc ?

Why is there so much poverty, unemployment, malnourishment, sickness etc in the world ? If God is
powerful and merciful, why does he not abolish these and give everyone a decent life ?
It is true that some scientists believed in God. But that only proves that scientific and unscientific ideas can co-exist in the same head, and it will take a long time, probably several generations, before unscientific ideas are altogether eliminated

All religions are superstitions and false. The truth lies in science, which is constantly developing.
If India is to progress, we must go over from religion to science

She carried it onto the porch. 

The fog had returned, thicker now, pressing against the railing. Down the path…. the path that, according to Helen, kept shortening, she saw a light. 

Not a lamp. 

A steady, low glow the color of a ship’s lantern seen through rain. It moved slowly, as if someone were walking the waterline, stopping now and then to listen.

Mara stepped off the porch. The boards did not creak. The air smelled of diesel and wet wool. She counted her steps. 

At thirty-one she reached the place where the path should have ended at the rocks. Instead the ground continued, firm under her boots, sloping gently downward. 

The light ahead of her paused. She heard, very clearly, the three strikes of a bell, then two more, closer than any buoy could be.
The light went out.

When she turned, the house was farther away than it should have been. Its windows were dark. The porch lamp she had left burning was gone. In its place, on the top step, sat the brass bell she still held in her hand, or thought she held. Her fingers were empty. 

The bell was on the step, and beside it, written in the thin film of salt the tide had left, were five words in a hand she recognized from the journals…

Do not answer it.

Behind her, out on the water that was no longer water, the bell struck once. Then it waited.
A flashlight beam cut through the fog from the road. “Harbor Police. Don’t move.”

Mara turned. 

A woman in a dark uniform stood at the edge of the yard, badge catching the weak light… Detective Lisa Nazzaro, 381. She kept one hand near her belt and studied the salt-written words, then the bell, then Mara’s empty hands.

“I’m Detective Lisa Nazzaro,” she said. 

Her voice was low, local. “Dispatch got a call about lights on the water and someone walking the point. You the one who inherited Helen’s place?”

Mara nodded. 

The detective’s eyes flicked past her toward the water, where the fog had thickened again. No light showed now.

“Helen called us twice last fall,” Detective Nazzaro said. “Same story. Path shortening. The bell that shouldn’t ring. 

We logged it and told her to stay off the rocks after dark. She stopped calling after that.” The officer stepped closer, boots crunching salt. “You hear it just now?”

“Three, then two,” Mara said. “Then one.”
Detective Nazzaro’s mouth tightened. She reached for her radio, then stopped. The static that came back, was not static. 

Under it, faint and precise, came the same pattern…three strikes, a pause, two more. Closer than the road. Closer than the house.

The detective lowered the radio without answering. She looked at the words in the salt, then at Mara.

“Get inside,” she said. “Lock the door. And whatever you do… please do not answer it.”

From the water the bell struck once more and held the note, waiting.

Mid-Journey——
above a rain-dark street,
the bandoneon breathed into the room.
A floorboard sighed beneath my shoe,
remembering a thousand other dances.

Then your palm settled 
between my shoulder blades——
a pressure scarcely heavier than breath.
I had not decided to move
when my heel began to rise.

Something in your hand had reached
something beneath my skin
before either of us could name it.

We turned. You paused.
In that pause, I felt the next step gathering,
quiet as a tide before it reaches shore.
When I stood still, I sensed your weight shifting;
when you stood still, the unfinished turn
went on turning inside my ribs.

No one had written this music.
A hesitation became a measure,
a breath held open the space between two notes.
We followed a score
our bodies were writing too quickly to read.

Where your hand met my back,
I could no longer tell
which of us had begun to sway.
Yet your hand remained your hand,
and my back, my back——
while the invisible boundary between them
moved with every breath.

Then the bandoneon fell silent.

Footsteps returned across the wooden floor.
But neither of us stepped away.
Beneath the quiet of our skin,
an unfinished measure went on.

And I wondered——
had we been dancing all along,
or was it the distance between us
that had finally learned to dance?

Of all the anachronistic and distorted, straw-man claptrap from @MichealMartinTD. 

How did the drafters of the 1916 proclamation at that time understand the cultural category 'Irish'? As culturally unique—handed down from generations past —and worthy of preservation (essentialism), or as culturally protean?

The opening paragraph of the proclamation strongly suggests cultural  uniqueness:
'In the name of God and of the dead generations from which she receives her old tradition of nationhood, Ireland, through us, summons her children to her flag and strikes for her freedom'.

The second paragraph even more so, as it refers to the undesirable historical impositions by foreign people and governments on Ireland: 
'We declare the right of the people of Ireland to the ownership of Ireland and to the unfettered control of Irish destinies, to be sovereign and indefeasible. The long usurpation of that right by a foreign people and government has not extinguished the right, nor can it ever be extinguished except by the destruction of the Irish people'.

In the decades ensuing the drafting of the proclamation, the drive for de-Anglicisation and re-Gaelicisation of the state—to counter the perceived ill effects of an imposed cultural imperialism—even yet more strongly suggests this pursuit of cultural essentialism or uniqueness by the political and other national establishments. 

It was within this latter cultural context that the drafters naively envisioned a theoretical society where all the nation's citizens would enjoy equality,  oblivious of the constructed differences fostered under historical colonialism and the imposition of an unequal union, then of 115 years standing. 

'The Republic guarantees religious and civil liberty, equal rights and equal opportunities to all its citizens, and declares its resolve to pursue the happiness and prosperity of the whole nation and of all its parts, cherishing all of the children of the nation equally, and oblivious of the differences carefully fostered by an alien Government, which have divided a minority from the majority in the past'.

Did those who drafted the proclamation desire a specifically Irish society and identity, culturally, socially, politically and economically better and more equal than that which preceded it? Certainly.  

Was the utopian dream achieved? No. For one thing a large cohort within the nation had  a different vision for Ireland, and hence partition. And even within the Free State, inequalities and cultural fault lines quickly became apparent. 

The utopian vision of Irishness shifted on the basis of four perceived idyllic purity criteria: Celtic, Irish-speaking, Rural and Catholic. Even sports were contaminated by these cultural constructs. 

Finally, did the proclamation's drafters envision ceding any newly-won sovereignty to foreign powers other than the United Kingdom? Certainly not. 

So the bottom line, @MichealMartinTD, is that you need to own your vision for Ireland and not anachronistically superimpose it on the intents of the proclamation drafters.

Here’s a distinction every investor should remember:

A great business is not automatically a great investment at every price.

Even a strong company can deliver disappointing returns if bought at an excessive valuation. 

Growth matters, but so does the price you pay for it.

Avoid letting greed or FOMO drive investment decisions.

Where could investors find opportunities?

Pankaj highlights areas such as manufacturing, consumer discretionary and financialisation.

But a promising sector alone isn’t enough. Investors still need to evaluate individual companies, their earnings potential and the price they are paying.

Then, look at the numbers.

A good business should generate healthy cash flows, maintain a sound balance sheet and use capital efficiently.

One useful metric discussed is the conversion of EBITDA into operating cash flow. 

Consistently converting around 70% or more over 3–5 years can be a helpful indicator to examine.

But how do you identify a business worth owning?

Start with the people running it.

Promoter quality, professional management, succession planning and the ability to execute matter. 

A company may operate in a promising industry, but its long-term performance also depends on how well it is managed.

Should investors wait for the market to hit the bottom before investing?

That’s a difficult game to play.

Instead of trying to predict the exact bottom, focus on the risk-reward of your investments over the next 3–5 years. 

The goal is to make decisions based on business fundamentals, not short-term market noise.

But does market weakness mean the Indian economy is losing momentum?

Not necessarily.

Auto demand, bank credit growth and GST collections offer important clues about economic activity. 

Pankaj’s point is to look beyond daily market movements and assess what is happening on the ground.

Valuations, slower earnings growth and better opportunities in other markets, particularly in AI and semiconductors, are among the factors influencing their decisions.

Higher energy costs can also add pressure.

Some technology stocks have fallen around 20%, while defence stocks have gained around 20%. Eicher has risen nearly 50%, while TCS has fallen close to 50%.

The lesson? Even in the same market, stock performance can look very different.

Ramkrishna Forgings Ltd. (RKFL): 7 growth triggers I’m tracking over the next 2–3 years

When I look at a company, I don’t just look at how much it is earning today. I also try to understand what could drive its earnings higher over the next few years.

RKFL manufactures forged components used in automobiles, commercial vehicles, railways and various engineering applications. It is one of India’s leading forging companies.

What makes the story interesting to me is that its potential growth doesn’t depend on just one big bet. There are multiple triggers that could work together over the next 2–3 years.

Let me break down the 7 things I’m watching.

1. Higher capacity utilisation: Sometimes, growth is already sitting inside the business.
This is probably the most important near-term trigger for RKFL.

The company’s capacity utilisation is currently around 68%. If it can move towards 80–85%, earnings could grow meaningfully without requiring a similar increase in investment.

Why?

Because factories have fixed costs. When production increases, those costs get spread across more units, which can improve operating margins.

Think of it this way: the factory is already built, the machinery is already installed, and a large part of the investment has already been made.

The key question is how much more the company can produce from the assets it already owns.

Of course, higher utilisation will depend on demand, customer orders and execution. But if these fall into place, this could become a powerful earnings driver.

 I’ll be watching capacity utilisation closely because it could drive both EBITDA growth and better cash generation.

2. Cold forging: An existing asset that could start contributing much more.
This is one of the more interesting parts of the RKFL story.

The company has around 25,000 MT of installed cold-forging capacity, but current utilisation is only around 40%.

In other words, a significant part of the capacity is still waiting to be fully utilised.

RKFL has reportedly secured orders from two large domestic passenger vehicle manufacturers and three international customers. If these orders translate into regular production, utilisation could move towards 70–75%.

Management’s indicated opportunity is roughly ₹200–250 crore in additional annual revenue.

The encouraging part is that the capacity is already in place. The company doesn't need to make the entire investment all over again to pursue this growth.

However, customer approvals, production ramp-up and actual order execution will determine how quickly the opportunity translates into revenue.

3. Casting: A business that could become much bigger.
RKFL is not just a forging story anymore. Casting is another segment worth tracking.

The company’s total casting capacity is now around 62,400 MT, while FY26 production was approximately 26,000 MT.

That leaves considerable room for growth if demand improves and the newer facility ramps up successfully.

The business has the potential to increase casting revenue towards ₹800–900 crore over time, compared with approximately ₹380 crore from the existing business in FY26, based on the opportunity outlined.

But there is another angle I find interesting: cross-selling.

Many customers who already purchase forgings from RKFL also have requirements for cast components.

That gives RKFL an opportunity to sell more products to customers with whom it already has relationships.

Acquiring a completely new customer can take time. Expanding business with an existing customer can sometimes be a more efficient route to growth.

4. Export recovery: Two markets that could make a difference.
Exports are another important piece of the puzzle.

North America was a drag on the business in FY26, largely because of the destocking cycle in Class 8 trucks.

If demand in the commercial vehicle market recovers, RKFL could benefit from higher orders and better utilisation of its export-oriented capacity.

There is also the European opportunity.

If the India–EU Free Trade Agreement eventually reduces or removes applicable duties on Indian forgings, RKFL could become more competitive against suppliers from Turkey and Eastern Europe.

The important point is that the company already has relationships with major European commercial vehicle manufacturers. Any improvement in trade competitiveness could potentially strengthen an existing business rather than require it to build one from scratch.

The Mexico plant is another piece to watch, particularly for its potential to serve North American customers closer to their manufacturing operations.

Of course, export recovery is not guaranteed. End-market demand, trade policy and the pace of customer orders will all matter.

A recovery in North America, combined with improved competitiveness in Europe, could provide another leg of growth.

5. Rail wheels JV: A potentially significant earnings contributor.
This is one of the longer-term opportunities I find worth tracking.

RKFL has a joint venture with Titagarh Rail Systems through Ramkrishna Titagarh Rail Wheels (RKTR).

The JV’s plant has an annual capacity of around 2.3 lakh wheels, with an initial contracted opportunity of approximately 40,000 wheels annually.

Production is expected to scale from FY27, and management has indicated potential first-year revenue of around ₹400–450 crore.

Beyond the initial domestic requirement, there could also be an opportunity to utilise the remaining capacity for exports, subject to orders and customer approvals.

But there is an important accounting distinction here.

The JV's entire revenue should not be treated as RKFL's consolidated revenue. The financial benefit to RKFL will largely depend on its share of the JV's profits and the applicable accounting treatment.

That means this opportunity could become an earnings contributor over time, even if its impact on reported consolidated revenue looks very different.

My view is Rail wheels could become an additional source of earnings, but the real numbers to track will be production ramp-up, profitability and RKFL's share of the JV's earnings.

6. Debt reduction: Not exciting, but potentially very valuable.
Debt reduction is an important part of the thesis because operating growth creates greater shareholder value when the company can retain more of the resulting profit.

RKFL's FY26 operating cash flow was approximately ₹840 crore, while net debt stood at around ₹1,900 crore in Q1 FY27. Management indicated that it was targeting a reduction of at least ₹500 crore in leverage during FY27, with net debt moving towards ₹1,500 crore by year-end.

Management also indicated FY27 capital expenditure of approximately ₹350 crore, excluding a further ₹20–30 crore associated with the first phase of the rail-wheel JV. This is significantly below the roughly ₹929 crore of capital expenditure cited for FY26, although actual expenditure and funding requirements will determine how much debt can ultimately be repaid.

The interest benefit is worth understanding. At an illustrative borrowing cost of 8.5%, reducing average debt by ₹500 crore for a full year would save approximately ₹42.5 crore in annual interest before considering taxes, fees or other changes. The actual benefit in FY27 may be smaller because the debt reduction occurs progressively during the year.

Lower debt can improve net profit, interest coverage and financial flexibility. It can also allow RKFL to fund maintenance and selective growth investments without repeatedly relying on additional borrowing.

But operating cash flow must be assessed alongside working capital and capex. A company can report strong EBITDA while still requiring substantial cash for receivables, inventory and expansion.

My view is that deleveraging is one of the most valuable supporting triggers. If RKFL increases utilization, generates cash and reduces debt simultaneously, the quality of earnings should improve- not just the headline growth rate.

7. Aluminium and aerospace: The optionality beyond the immediate growth story.

This is where I start thinking beyond the next two or three years.

RKFL has started bulk production of aluminium forgings for global EV customers.

Aluminium forgings can command much higher realisations per kilogram than conventional steel forgings. The opportunity is interesting because even relatively modest volumes could contribute meaningfully if pricing, margins and customer demand are favourable.

Then there is aerospace.

The company has installed forging capabilities for materials such as titanium and Inconel and is pursuing aerospace opportunities through RFQs.

However, I would be careful here. Quoting for an order is not the same as winning it, and winning a programme does not immediately translate into substantial revenue.

Until meaningful orders materialise, I would treat aerospace as a potential future opportunity rather than a core part of the current investment case.

Aluminium could contribute to the growth story sooner, while aerospace remains a longer-term opportunity that needs to be demonstrated through actual orders and execution.
________________________________________

A growth opportunity is not the same as growth that has already been delivered.

Some of these triggers are relatively near-term, while others depend on customer approvals, market recovery, order wins and execution over several years.

For me, the real test will be whether these opportunities translate into higher utilisation, sustainable margins, stronger cash flows and a healthier balance sheet.

And, ultimately, whether the current valuation adequately compensates investors for the risks involved.

Before asking investors to examine a fund’s WORST returns, perhaps fund managers should examine their OWN WORST investment decisions.

Quoting a -61% SIP XIRR over one year, -38% over two years and -23% over three years is not, by itself, evidence of a sound investment strategy.

And celebrating a subsequent recovery does not retrospectively validate every decision made during the decline.

A recovery is an outcome. It is NOT proof that the preceding investment decisions were right.

Your argument essentially asks investors to endure the damage for 7–10 years because the market may eventually recover.

But here are the questions you conveniently leave unanswered:

1. WHO is accountable for the lost decade?

You acknowledge that there was a phase when investors had not grown their money even after seven years, and that the worst 10-year return was just 4%.

Four per cent over a decade is not a triumph of long-term investing. Depending on inflation and the timing of cash flows, it can represent a substantial loss of purchasing power.

A child entering school today could be entering university when that decade ends. Who will compensate the family if the money earmarked for education has failed to grow meaningfully?

2. WHY should investors accept the entire drawdown as inevitable?

Nobody expects a fund manager to predict every market top and bottom.

But distinguishing a genuine reversal from a temporary pullback, assessing deteriorating price structures and managing downside exposure are legitimate parts of investment analysis.

Simple RAW PRICE ACTION had been signalling serious deterioration in several major stocks, including HDFC Bank, Reliance, ITC, TCS, Infosys, HCL Technologies, Tata Motors, IEX, PB Fintech and CMS Info.

Yet fund houses continued to hold or add exposure to several of these stocks.

The relevant question is not whether the market eventually recovers. It is whether the risks were adequately recognised when investors' money was being deployed.

3. WHY is every dip presented as an opportunity, but every prolonged decline explained away using a 7–10-year horizon?

A lower price does not automatically mean a better investment. Averaging down does not automatically demonstrate conviction. And a SIP is a method of investing—not immunity against poor asset selection or prolonged capital erosion.

Investors deserve to know whether the underlying price structure and risk-reward profile justify continued accumulation.

4. YOUR OWN INDUSTRY'S PORTFOLIOS DESERVE THE SAME SCRUTINY.

HDFC AMC's reported accumulation in PB Fintech, PPFAS's reported buying in IEX during Q2 2025, and its reported purchase of approximately 20 lakh CMS Info shares in October 2025 all raise legitimate questions about timing, downside assessment and capital allocation.

The actual holdings, transaction prices and portfolio-level losses must be verified. But these questions cannot be dismissed merely by telling investors to remain patient.

5. AND FINALLY, YOUR FAVOURITE DISCLAIMER.

“Past performance is not indicative of future returns.”

Absolutely correct.

Then why should investors accept past recoveries as evidence that the next recovery will arrive within their investment horizon?

If past performance cannot guarantee future returns, neither can a historical recovery guarantee that the next decade will compensate investors adequately for the risks they take today.

An FD and an equity mutual fund serve different purposes. But investors choosing equity deserve more than a lecture on patience after suffering years of capital erosion.

They deserve disciplined capital allocation, honest risk assessment and managers willing to acknowledge when their investment decisions deserve scrutiny.

No one is demanding that you predict every bottom. We are asking why investors must bear the full consequences when your investment process fails to recognise the risks.

The central idea is simple:
Don't just ask, “How strong is this company's moat?”
Ask three harder questions:
Who can break that moat?
Who captures the profits it creates?
Can the company reinvest those profits to become more valuable over time?
CDSL, IEX, IRCTC, Asian Paints, Pidilite and Coal India illustrate very different answers.
That is what makes monopoly analysis interesting: the same market dominance can produce very different economic outcomes.

Coal India illustrates why even enormous resources and profits can fail to tell the full story.
The company controls roughly 75% of domestic coal production, according to the research.
Yet more than 80–85% of its coal volume is committed under long-term fuel supply agreements at regulated prices.
The research compares typical agreement realisations of ₹1,500–₹1,600 per tonne with e-auction prices of ₹2,500–₹4,000.
The company has substantial scale, but it cannot freely convert all that scale into market-price earnings.

CDSL also shows why small fees can support a powerful business.

According to the research, around 38–40% of its revenue comes from recurring annual issuer charges.

Its settlement debit fee was standardised at ₹3.50 per transaction following SEBI's October 2024 “True to Label” circular.

When a fee is tiny compared with the value of the activity it supports, customers may have little reason to change their behaviour.

The infrastructure remains useful even when pricing rules change.
